traveler.mora.bio: Hi! I’m Mora, from Buenos Aires. I have a notebook full of hand-drawn maps and there’s no bus I can’t figure out. Will you join me around the world?
traveler.nilo.bio: Hi! I’m Nilo. I left Berlin with my aviator cap, my goggles and Grandma’s red scarf. I love flying in a balloon and collecting passport stamps.
traveler.ren.bio: Hi! I’m Ren, from Kyoto. I’ve walked among bamboo since I was little and I always carry my camera. I want to take a selfie in every corner of the planet.
tuto.1.p: You don’t move him: in this game your finger doesn’t push the character, it builds the path he will run on.
tuto.2.p: Tap any lane and Nilo heads straight there, even from the other side. Or hold your finger and drag to follow it.
tuto.3.p: If there’s an obstacle in your lane, build the path around it before you get there. Boat, balloon and train carry you over sea, sky and rails: keep building ahead of them.
tuto.customs.p: Some tiles are customs gates in a region color. With that color's passport equipped you pass and earn coins; otherwise the tile is a rock. Equip one in your backpack. A free path is always left.
tuto.mov.p: From here on, some obstacles switch lanes. Build your path where they don't go, or tap the freeze button to stop them for a few seconds.
tuto.rail.p: On rows with switch arrows, the diversion takes you one lane. If there is a barrier that way, you will crash: aim diagonally against the switch to keep going straight.
tuto.tide.p: On rows with arrows, the current drags you one lane. If there is a rock that way, you will crash: aim diagonally against the current to keep going straight.
tuto.wind.p: On windy rows, the gust drags you one lane. If there is an obstacle that way, you will crash: aim diagonally against the wind to keep going straight.
chest.panelSub: WHAT YOU FOUND ON THE WAY
chest.how: They appear on the track and when you complete missions, and you keep them even if you lose. Wooden chests open instantly; silver takes 20 min and gold 2 h. You have {n} slots: when they're full, new chests turn into a few coins.
chest.proHint: With PRO they all open instantly.
chest.has.plata: Coins, an item and maybe a souvenir
chest.has.oro: Lots of coins, 2 items and souvenirs
mission.howMult: Your level multiplies the points of every run. Each completed mission gives you a silver chest.
ficha.nilo.why: He found the flight logbook of his grandfather, the pilot who disappeared over South America in 1974.
ficha.nilo.quote: The sky is the only country without borders.
ficha.nilo.likes: The sound of old engines, coffee without sugar, cities at night.
ficha.nilo.dreamHint: Where water falls from the clouds.
ficha.mora.why: She had never left Buenos Aires. Her brother Tomi left three years ago and sends her postcards with no return address: she sets out to find him and to see the world with her own eyes.
ficha.mora.quote: If you don’t know where you’re going, any bus will do.
ficha.sipho.why: He will be the last keeper of his lighthouse and wants to meet the radio voices his father used to talk to.
ficha.sipho.quote: A light is useless if nobody looks at it.
ficha.minji.why: She was the best dancer at her academy in Seoul until she froze at the final, in front of thousands. Now she dances alone in the streets of the world… and someone is posting every dance online.
ficha.minji.quote: Even if nobody’s watching, I dance.
ficha.tuk.why: He found a letter from 1979 that was never delivered and swore to get it where it belongs.
ficha.tuk.quote: A letter that never arrives is a question with no answer.
ficha.layla.why: She follows the guide to desert skies left by her mom, an astronomer who stopped answering her phone.
ficha.layla.quote: The good light always comes if you know how to wait.
ficha.cal.why: A year ago his climbing partner fell while Cal was belaying him. Eli hasn’t spoken to him since. Now his list of summits has arrived, with a note: “You climb them.”
ficha.anaya.why: Her grandmother is losing her sight and wants to see, one last time, a color she lost sixty years ago. Anaya sets off around the world to find it… on wheels.
ficha.anaya.quote: Every place has a color nobody has named.
hist.nilo.title: Opa’s Logbook
hist.nilo.1.title: The Attic
hist.nilo.1.hint: It all starts at home: go back to Berlin, Nilo’s city.
hist.nilo.1.l1: I went back to Berlin and climbed up to Grandma’s attic. I only wanted Opa’s goggles.
hist.nilo.1.l2: But there was something else in the box: his flight logbook. Seven places marked in red ink.
hist.nilo.1.l3: The last page has been torn out. And on every page there is a single letter, squeezed against the edge: M.
hist.nilo.1.l4: Opa disappeared in 1974, flying over South America. They never found the plane.
hist.nilo.1.l5: Grandma says I shouldn’t read it. That’s why I’m going to read every word. First stop: Paris.
hist.nilo.1.back: Today I found Opa’s logbook. Grandma asked me to leave it in the box. I couldn’t. First page: a café in Paris and a letter, M. Here I go.
hist.nilo.2.title: Two Coffees
hist.nilo.2.hint: A café where there was always one cup too many.
hist.nilo.2.l1: The Paris page has the address of a café. It’s still open, with the same wicker chairs.
hist.nilo.2.l2: Those goggles? I know them. Your grandfather came every Tuesday and ordered two coffees.
hist.nilo.2.l3: One always went cold. She arrived late, always running. I never learned her name.
hist.nilo.2.l4: For M. It has to be for M.
hist.nilo.2.l5: One day he left a huge tip and a note: “I’m going to Istanbul. If she comes, tell her I’ll wait for her there.”
hist.nilo.2.back: The waiter is eighty and recognized the goggles before he recognized me. Opa ordered two coffees and she always came late. Who were you, M.?
hist.nilo.3.title: M.’s Photo
hist.nilo.3.hint: A photo from 1960 that nobody came to collect.
hist.nilo.3.l1: Tucked between the pages of the logbook was a receipt: a photo studio in Galata, 1960.
hist.nilo.3.l2: My grandfather kept every negative nobody picked up. Look at this one: a pilot and a girl, laughing.
hist.nilo.3.l3: She has a scarf with an M embroidered on it. And Opa… I never saw him smile like that in any photo at home.
hist.nilo.3.l4: Something is written on the back in pencil. “Marrakech. The souk. Wait for me.”
hist.nilo.3.l5: Opa was following her around the world. Or she was following him.
hist.nilo.3.back: Opa was 24 in the photo. He has my same crooked smile. Nobody at home ever told me. She laughed with her eyes closed.
hist.nilo.4.title: The Letter in the Souk
hist.nilo.4.hint: A door with a little plane painted on it.
hist.nilo.4.l1: That lamp stall has Opa’s little plane painted on the door.
hist.nilo.4.l2: My father kept this letter for sixty years. He said a German pilot would come for it.
hist.nilo.4.l3: He never came. His grandson did. Sometimes that’s enough.
hist.nilo.4.l4: “M.: if you wait for me, I’ll tell you where the water falls from the sky.”
hist.nilo.4.l5: The letter never left this place. So how did M. know where to go?
hist.nilo.4.l6: My father used to say the pilot left here for Rio de Janeiro. That a storm was waiting for him.
hist.nilo.4.back: The letter never reached M. Opa left it here and kept flying. Did she wait for him? And what was he going to tell her where the water falls from the sky?
hist.nilo.5.title: Landing Blind
hist.nilo.5.hint: A storm that closed the sky for three days.
hist.nilo.5.l1: The Rio page has a single word, written so hard it tore the paper: “storm”.
hist.nilo.5.l2: 1961. A pilot landed blind in the middle of a storm. I saw it myself from the tower.
hist.nilo.5.l3: He shouted that someone was waiting for him in Buenos Aires. We closed the sky for three days.
hist.nilo.5.l4: Three days late. Again. A cold coffee, an unsent letter, a storm.
hist.nilo.5.l5: But that time she was the one who came. The girl with the scarf stepped off the first flight after the storm. They flew north together, to the middle of the world.
hist.nilo.5.back: Three days of storm and she still came looking for him. I hope someone waits for me like that one day.
hist.nilo.6.title: One Foot in Each Half
hist.nilo.6.hint: The line that splits the world in two.
hist.nilo.6.l1: One foot in the north, one foot in the south. The line runs right between my boots.
hist.nilo.6.l2: The notebook changes here. There’s a second handwriting now, round, signing M.
hist.nilo.6.l3: “One foot in each half, like us: you from the sky, me from the ground. Tomorrow, the waterfall.”
hist.nilo.6.l4: What happened at the waterfall is on the missing page. And why Opa never came back, too.
hist.nilo.6.back: A second handwriting appeared in the notebook today, round, M.’s. It looks familiar and I can’t tell why.
hist.nilo.7.title: Where the Water Falls from the Sky
hist.nilo.7.hint: Where water falls from the clouds.
hist.nilo.7.l1: Angel Falls. Almost a thousand meters of water falling from the clouds. Opa was right: it looks like the sky is breaking.
hist.nilo.7.l2: There’s a rock with the little plane carved into it. Underneath, a rusty tin.
hist.nilo.7.l3: Inside is the torn-out page. At the top, in M.’s round hand: “Yes. May 14, 1961.” Below, Opa’s, from 1974:
hist.nilo.7.l4: “M.: thirteen years today. I came to leave this where you said yes, so we can read it together next year. The sky is turning black; I’ll make it anyway. I owe you a honeymoon: the island of the moai. Yours, A.”
hist.nilo.7.l5: Opa didn’t leave. The storm wouldn’t let him come back. And he owed someone a honeymoon. I think I know who.
hist.nilo.7.back: Opa didn’t abandon us: the sky didn’t let him come home. And that round handwriting… I’ve seen it my whole life on the fridge door.
hist.nilo.8.title: The Island
hist.nilo.8.l1: Opa’s letter brought me to the moai. This time I didn’t come alone.
hist.nilo.8.l2: Grandma stepped off the plane with an old scarf over her hair. It has an M embroidered on it.
hist.nilo.8.l3: I asked you not to read it because I never could. Fifty years waiting for that page.
hist.nilo.8.l5: Your grandfather called me M. because he was late even for saying my whole name.
hist.nilo.8.l6: Order two coffees. This time we made it in time.
hist.nilo.8.l7: I’ll order three, Grandma. One is for Opa.
hist.nilo.8.back: Grandma laughed with her eyes closed, just like in the Istanbul photo. I read her the last page out loud. We made it in time.
diary.soonSub: Every traveler will have their own diary of postcards.
ficha.mora.likes: Night buses, the bandoneon, buttery medialunas.
ficha.mora.fears: Spending her whole life looking at the world on postcards.
ficha.mora.dreamHint: The green sky she used to draw as a kid.
hist.mora.title: Tomi’s Postcards
hist.mora.1.title: Above the bed
hist.mora.1.hint: It all starts at home: go back to Buenos Aires, Mora’s city.
hist.mora.1.l1: I’ve never even crossed the river. I know the world from the postcards Tomi has sent since he left, three years ago.
hist.mora.1.l2: None of them has a return address. I keep them stuck above my bed, in the order they arrived.
hist.mora.1.l3: Today I noticed something: each one comes from a place a little farther than the last.
hist.mora.1.l4: As if someone were teaching me to walk.
hist.mora.1.l5: On the back of the first one, in tiny letters: “Start here, squirt.” It’s from Montevideo.
hist.mora.1.back: Twelve postcards above my bed, each one a little farther away. Tomorrow I’m taking the boat. Alone.
hist.mora.2.title: The bandoneon
hist.mora.2.hint: The first postcard: cross the river.
hist.mora.2.l1: My first trip alone. One hour on the boat and the river is already a different color.
hist.mora.2.l2: Tomi’s sister? He played here a whole summer. He told me you’d come one day.
hist.mora.2.l3: I didn’t believe him. He said you were scared of the bus, even.
hist.mora.2.l4: I was. I still am. But here I am.
hist.mora.2.l5: He left you this: a photo of a colorful balcony by the sea. On the back: “The second one is farther. Dare you?”
hist.mora.2.back: Tomi knew I’d come before I did. Next is a colorful balcony by the sea.
hist.mora.3.title: The balcony
hist.mora.3.hint: A colorful balcony by the sea.
hist.mora.3.l1: No postcard warns you about the heat, the salt, or the music on every corner.
hist.mora.3.l2: That balcony is mine. Your brother rented the room upstairs for a month.
hist.mora.3.l3: He wrote postcards every morning. Some he sent, and some he kept in a tin.
hist.mora.3.l4: And why did he never put a return address?
hist.mora.3.l5: I asked him the same thing. He said: “If she knows where I am, she’ll just wait for me to come back. And I want her to come.”
hist.mora.3.back: Tomi leaves no return address so I won’t just wait. He took the tin to the city in the clouds. What’s inside?
hist.mora.4.title: The city in the clouds
hist.mora.4.l1: I’m out of breath, and it’s not the altitude. From up here, Buenos Aires is a dot you can’t even see.
hist.mora.4.l2: Your brother always sat on this step.
hist.mora.4.l3: He said this is where he realized he wasn’t looking for places: he was looking for things to show you.
hist.mora.4.l4: I don’t know anymore if I’m climbing for him or for me.
hist.mora.4.l5: Both count. He asked me to tell you this: “The next one is the hardest. Bundle up.”
hist.mora.4.back: Today I climbed higher than ever and I wasn’t scared. “Bundle up”… Where are you sending me now, Tomi?
hist.mora.5.title: The end of the world
hist.mora.5.hint: Bundle up: the next one is the hardest.
hist.mora.5.l1: The end of the world. The wind pushes you like it doesn’t want you to go on.
hist.mora.5.l2: I have a letter for the girl in the red beret. I’ve kept it for two years.
hist.mora.5.l3: It has a single line: “If you made it this far, I don’t need to wait for you anywhere anymore.”
hist.mora.5.l4: And a ticket, with a date, to a place that isn’t on any of his postcards.
hist.mora.5.l5: Reykjavík. The green sky I used to draw as a kid. I never told anyone.
hist.mora.5.back: A dated ticket to the green sky I drew as a kid. How did he know? Will he be there?
hist.mora.6.title: The lights
hist.mora.6.hint: The green sky Mora used to draw as a kid.
hist.mora.6.l1: It’s midnight, the date on the ticket. Nothing happens and nobody comes.
hist.mora.6.l2: Until the sky lights up green, like a match. For a second I forget who I was looking for.
hist.mora.6.l4: You drew it on every wall. I thought if you made it here alone, you wouldn’t be afraid of anything anymore.
hist.mora.6.l5: He gave me the tin. There’s a postcard with no picture that only says: “Home.”
hist.mora.6.back: I found Tomi under a green sky. In the tin there’s a postcard with no picture that says “Home.” We’re going back.
hist.mora.7.title: Home
hist.mora.7.hint: A postcard with no picture that only says “Home.”
hist.mora.7.l1: We came back together. The house is the same. I’m the one who changed.
hist.mora.7.l3: Hi, Mom. I brought you the traveler.
hist.mora.7.l4: I took the postcards down from above my bed and stuck them on a map. Where there are none, there’s still a lot of map left.
hist.mora.7.l5: The next postcard is mine to send. With a return address.
hist.mora.7.back: The postcards aren’t above my bed anymore: they’re on a map full of gaps. I’m going to fill them.
hist.mora.8.title: A place with no postcard
hist.mora.8.hint: A place that isn’t on any postcard.
hist.mora.8.l1: I made a new rule: go somewhere that isn’t on any of Tomi’s postcards.
hist.mora.8.l2: The smoke that thunders. The water sounds like the whole world applauding.
hist.mora.8.l3: I told you some places don’t fit on a postcard.
hist.mora.8.l4: I took a picture anyway, for Mom’s wall. From: Mora. To: the next one.
hist.mora.8.l5: First postcard of the new list. From: Mora, Inés and Tomi. This time we signed it.
hist.mora.8.back: First postcard with a return address: Mora. Destination: the next one.
ficha.sipho.likes: The hum of the radio, rooibos tea, stormy nights.
ficha.sipho.fears: That the light goes out and nobody notices.
ficha.sipho.dreamHint: The other light, at the bottom of everything.
hist.sipho.title: The Lighthouse Voices
hist.sipho.1.title: Dad’s frequency
hist.sipho.1.hint: It all starts at home: go back to Cape Town, Sipho’s city.
hist.sipho.1.l1: Next year they’re automating the lighthouse. I’ll be the last keeper in Cape Town.
hist.sipho.1.l2: Dad talked on the radio every night. In his notebook he wrote down voices from ports all over the world.
hist.sipho.1.l3: I never saw their faces. I only know their names, their cities and what time they called.
hist.sipho.1.l4: Last night, at three o’clock sharp, the radio came alive on his frequency: “Cape Town, do you copy?”
hist.sipho.1.l5: Dad died a year ago, and someone doesn’t know. The first voice in the notebook is from Zanzibar.
hist.sipho.1.back: Someone is still calling Dad at three in the morning. I’m going to find his voices, one by one.
hist.sipho.2.title: The shipyard
hist.sipho.2.hint: The first voice in the notebook: a dhow shipyard.
hist.sipho.2.l1: Zanzibar smells of cloves. The voice in the notebook came from a dhow shipyard.
hist.sipho.2.l2: You’re the lighthouse keeper’s son? Your dad taught me to talk on the radio when I was ten.
hist.sipho.2.l3: But there was someone he talked to more than anyone. He never said her name.
hist.sipho.2.l4: So what did he call her?
hist.sipho.2.l5: “The lady of the other light.” Ask Manuel, in Lisbon. He heard everything.
hist.sipho.2.back: Dad talked to someone more than anyone: “the lady of the other light.” Another light? Another lighthouse?
hist.sipho.3.title: The radio operator
hist.sipho.3.hint: Someone who heard everything from the ships.
hist.sipho.3.l1: Lisbon rises and falls like the waves. Manuel was a ship’s radio operator for forty years.
hist.sipho.3.l2: The lady of the other light… Of course. She always signed off the same way: “Good night from the bottom of everything.”
hist.sipho.3.l3: Your dad would laugh and answer: “Good night from the tip of Africa.”
hist.sipho.3.l4: The bottom of everything? The bottom of what?
hist.sipho.3.l5: Bergur, in Reykjavík, recorded one of those talks. He can play it for you.
hist.sipho.3.back: “Good night from the bottom of everything.” There’s a recording of Dad in Reykjavík.
hist.sipho.4.title: The tape
hist.sipho.4.hint: A tape with Dad’s voice on it.
hist.sipho.4.l1: In Reykjavík the wind whistles through Bergur’s antenna like a badly tuned radio.
hist.sipho.4.l3: It’s Dad’s voice: “One day I’ll come and see your light. I promise.”
hist.sipho.4.l4: He never went. He never left the lighthouse.
hist.sipho.4.l5: She answered something else, but the tape cuts off. Jae-won, in Busan, heard the whole thing.
hist.sipho.4.back: I heard Dad promise to go see a light. He never went. What did she answer?
hist.sipho.5.title: The fishing boat
hist.sipho.5.hint: Someone who heard the whole tape.
hist.sipho.5.l1: Busan is a thousand boats and a thousand lights. Jae-won has been on the radio from his fishing boat for thirty years.
hist.sipho.5.l2: She told him: “If one day you don’t answer, I’ll call your son.”
hist.sipho.5.l3: A month ago she called me. She said her lighthouse is going dark this year too.
hist.sipho.5.l4: Then she doesn’t have much time left to call.
hist.sipho.5.l5: Ruth, in Sydney, has her call sign written down. Go quickly.
hist.sipho.5.back: “If one day you don’t answer, I’ll call your son.” And her lighthouse goes dark this year too.
hist.sipho.6.title: The call sign
hist.sipho.6.hint: The written call sign of the other light.
hist.sipho.6.l1: Sydney is the farthest from home I’ve ever been. You can still hear the sea.
hist.sipho.6.l2: Here it is, in your dad’s handwriting and mine: the call sign of a lighthouse in Argentina.
hist.sipho.6.l3: “The bottom of everything” was literal, love. The end of the world.
hist.sipho.6.l4: Ushuaia. The other light was the lighthouse at the end of the world.
hist.sipho.6.l5: She asked me, if anyone from Cape Town ever turned up, to tell them to hurry.
hist.sipho.6.back: The other light was the lighthouse at the end of the world. And she asked me to hurry.
hist.sipho.7.title: The other light
hist.sipho.7.hint: The other light, at the bottom of everything.
hist.sipho.7.l1: The lighthouse at the end of the world is red and white, tiny, on a rocky island. Just like Dad’s, but upside down.
hist.sipho.7.l2: I knew you’d come. You have his voice.
hist.sipho.7.l3: Your dad asked me something years ago: if one day he didn’t answer, I should call you. So you’d leave the lighthouse.
hist.sipho.7.l4: Is that why you called at three in the morning?
hist.sipho.7.l5: That’s why. A light is no use if nobody looks at it. Now go and look at the others.
hist.sipho.7.back: Elena called because Dad asked her to: so I’d leave the lighthouse. Now it’s my turn to look at the other lights.
hist.sipho.8.title: Over and out
hist.sipho.8.l1: It’s the last night before they automate the lighthouse. I switch on Dad’s radio.
hist.sipho.8.l2: I call every voice in the notebook: Zanzibar, Lisbon, Reykjavík, Busan, Sydney, Ushuaia.
hist.sipho.8.l4: I switch off the lamp with my own hands. The automatic one comes on by itself, without me.
hist.sipho.8.l5: “Cape Town, over and out. Tomorrow I set off.”
hist.sipho.8.back: Cape Town, over and out. Tomorrow I set off.
ficha.minji.likes: K-pop at full volume, her turquoise headphones, midnight ramyeon.
ficha.minji.fears: Standing still when the music starts.
ficha.minji.dreamHint: A stage with a thousand screens.
hist.minji.title: Lost Steps
hist.minji.1.title: The final
hist.minji.1.hint: It all starts at home: go back to Seoul, Minji’s city.
hist.minji.1.l1: Three minutes of music and I didn’t move. Thousands of people watching.
hist.minji.1.l2: Since that day I can’t step onto a stage. I quit the academy.
hist.minji.1.l3: Last night a nameless account, @lost_steps, posted a video of me as a kid, dancing in the subway.
hist.minji.1.l4: The caption says: “This is the Minji I know. First stop: Tokyo.”
hist.minji.1.l5: Nobody has that video. Who is it?
hist.minji.1.back: Someone has a video of me as a kid dancing in the subway. First stop: Tokyo. Who is it?
hist.minji.2.title: The crossing
hist.minji.2.l1: In Shibuya the light stays green for forty seconds. I danced in the middle of the crossing until it turned red.
hist.minji.2.l2: People clapped from the sidewalks. My legs were shaking, but I didn’t freeze.
hist.minji.2.l3: That night, @lost_steps posted the dance, filmed from above.
hist.minji.2.l4: “You have to learn to dance with fear. Madrid.”
hist.minji.2.back: Someone was there, watching me, and posted the dance. Now they’re sending me to Madrid.
hist.minji.3.title: The desplante
hist.minji.3.l1: In flamenco you stand still too, girl. But on purpose.
hist.minji.3.l2: It’s called a desplante: you stop, you stamp the floor, and the silence is yours.
hist.minji.3.l3: My silence at the final wasn’t on purpose.
hist.minji.3.l4: Now it is. Oh, your class was already paid for: a Korean girl, with a camera. She left you this: “Havana.”
hist.minji.3.back: My flamenco class was paid for by a Korean girl with a camera. Do I know her?
hist.minji.4.title: The song
hist.minji.4.hint: A city where music pours out of the windows.
hist.minji.4.l1: In Havana, music pours out of every window. An old man pulled me into a salsa in the street.
hist.minji.4.l2: The girl with the camera asked us to play this song for you.
hist.minji.4.l3: It’s the song from the final. I froze for a second.
hist.minji.4.back: I danced to the song from the final and didn’t stop. Only someone who was there knows that song.
hist.minji.5.title: The headband
hist.minji.5.l1: The samba school rehearsal goes on until dawn. Nobody watches you: everybody dances.
hist.minji.5.l2: On the bench where I left my backpack there was a headband from my academy.
hist.minji.5.l4: Hana was my best friend. And she was the one who won the final.
hist.minji.5.back: The headband says Hana: my best friend, the one who won the final. Why is she following me?
hist.minji.6.title: The tango
hist.minji.6.hint: A dance you can’t dance alone.
hist.minji.6.l1: Tango isn’t danced alone, kid. You dance it with someone who holds you up.
hist.minji.6.l2: I danced with an eighty-year-old stranger and barely stepped on his feet.
hist.minji.6.l3: That night, @lost_steps posted the video with another message.
hist.minji.6.l4: “New York. Saturday. Times Square. This time you won’t dance alone.”
hist.minji.6.back: New York, Saturday, Times Square. This time I won’t dance alone.
hist.minji.7.title: Times Square
hist.minji.7.l1: Times Square: a thousand screens and a thousand people. The music starts and I freeze again.
hist.minji.7.l2: Then Hana steps out of the crowd, puts the camera on the ground and starts dancing next to me.
hist.minji.7.l3: I won because you froze. I never forgave myself.
hist.minji.7.l4: I wanted the world to see the real Minji. The one who danced in the subway.
hist.minji.7.l5: This time I didn’t freeze. Because I wasn’t alone.
hist.minji.7.back: In Times Square I didn’t freeze, because I wasn’t alone. Hana was there.
hist.minji.8.title: The duo
hist.minji.8.l1: We went back to the academy. This year there’s a duo category.
hist.minji.8.l4: I used to say: “Even if nobody’s watching, I dance.” Today, let them watch.
hist.minji.8.back: I used to dance even if nobody was watching. Today, let them watch.
ficha.tuk.likes: The smell of old paper, the harbor wind, puffins.
ficha.tuk.fears: That a letter stays without its owner forever.
ficha.tuk.dreamHint: The mailbox at the end of the world.
hist.tuk.title: The 1979 Letter
hist.tuk.1.title: The lost mailbag
hist.tuk.1.hint: It all starts at home: go back to Reykjavík, Tuk’s city.
hist.tuk.1.l1: They’re renovating the old harbor post office. Behind a wall, a mailbag from 1979 turned up.
hist.tuk.1.l2: Every letter got delivered, forty-five years late. All but one.
hist.tuk.1.l3: “To Ingrid Larsen, Lisbon.” No sender: just an S and a little puffin drawing.
hist.tuk.1.l4: On the back, in a hurry: “Urgent. Before summer.”
hist.tuk.1.l5: A letter that never arrives is a question with no answer. I’m taking it myself.
hist.tuk.1.back: An undelivered letter from 1979: “To Ingrid Larsen, Lisbon,” signed with an S. Who is S.?
hist.tuk.2.title: The old address
hist.tuk.2.l1: There’s a café at the letter’s address now. Luckily, it still has the same owner.
hist.tuk.2.l2: Ingrid? The Icelandic girl on the third floor. She waited all that summer for a letter from her sister.
hist.tuk.2.l3: She came down to the mailbox every morning. Nothing ever came.
hist.tuk.2.l5: Then she went to study in Scotland. Seabirds, I think.
hist.tuk.2.back: S. is Ingrid’s sister. Ingrid waited a whole summer for her, then left for Scotland.
hist.tuk.3.title: The dedication
hist.tuk.3.l1: Edinburgh is all stone and wind. In the university library there’s Ingrid’s thesis, about puffins.
hist.tuk.3.l2: There’s a dedication on the first page.
hist.tuk.3.l3: “For my sister, who never wrote back.”
hist.tuk.3.l4: She did write back. And I have the answer, right here in my pocket.
hist.tuk.3.l5: Ingrid went off to work with the penguins in Cape Town.
hist.tuk.3.back: “For my sister, who never wrote back.” Forty-five years thinking her sister didn’t love her.
hist.tuk.4.title: The colony
hist.tuk.4.hint: A beach with more penguins than people.
hist.tuk.4.l1: On the penguin beach there are more penguins than people.
hist.tuk.4.l2: Ingrid worked with me for ten years. She hardly ever talked about Iceland.
hist.tuk.4.l3: Only once she told me: “If a letter from home ever reaches me, I’ll go back.”
hist.tuk.4.l4: It reached her late. But it reached her.
hist.tuk.4.l5: Then she moved to Sydney, to run an ocean institute.
hist.tuk.4.back: “If a letter from home ever reaches me, I’ll go back.” Ingrid kept moving farther from Iceland.
hist.tuk.5.title: The institute
hist.tuk.5.l1: There’s a photo of Ingrid on the institute wall. In it she’s my age, with a stuffed puffin on her desk.
hist.tuk.5.l2: She retired last year. Said she was going to the end of the world, to count penguins until her last day.
hist.tuk.5.l4: Ushuaia. If you go, take her a coat. And patience: she doesn’t like talking about Iceland.
hist.tuk.5.back: Ingrid went to the end of the world to count penguins. I’m going to find her.
hist.tuk.6.title: The answer
hist.tuk.6.hint: The end of the world, counting penguins.
hist.tuk.6.l1: Ingrid is tiny, white-haired, with the same look as in the Sydney photo.
hist.tuk.6.l2: I gave her the letter. She opened it with shaking hands.
hist.tuk.6.l3: “Forgive me. Come for Mom’s birthday. I’ll be waiting at the harbor. S.”
hist.tuk.6.l4: Mom died that summer. I didn’t go because I thought Sólveig didn’t want me there.
hist.tuk.6.l5: Sólveig… The lady who feeds the puffins at Reykjavík harbor is called Sólveig.
hist.tuk.6.back: I delivered the letter to Ingrid. Her sister’s name is Sólveig… and she’s alive, at my harbor.
hist.tuk.7.title: The harbor
hist.tuk.7.l1: We came back together. Sólveig was at the harbor, like every morning, with her bag of fish.
hist.tuk.7.l3: Your letter reached me. Forty-five years late.
hist.tuk.7.l4: I waited for you at this harbor every summer.
hist.tuk.7.l5: A letter that never arrives is a question with no answer. This one has its answer now.
hist.tuk.7.back: Two sisters at Reykjavík harbor. A letter that finally has its answer.
hist.tuk.8.title: From: Tuk
hist.tuk.8.l1: The two sisters went back to the café at the old address. Dona Graça cried more than they did.
hist.tuk.8.l2: This time we wrote the letter together.
hist.tuk.8.l3: With a return address, just in case.
hist.tuk.8.l4: It’s the first letter of my life addressed to me: “For Tuk, the postman who never gave up.”
hist.tuk.8.back: The first letter with my name on it: “For Tuk, the postman who never gave up.”
ficha.layla.likes: Moonless nights, cardamom tea, her folding telescope.
ficha.layla.fears: A cloud covering the star just as it appears.
ficha.layla.dreamHint: The oldest desert in the world.
hist.layla.title: Comet L-18
hist.layla.1.title: The silence
hist.layla.1.hint: It all starts at home: go back to Amman, Layla’s city.
hist.layla.1.back: “If I’m not back before your birthday, follow the guide.” What is L-18? And where is Mom?
hist.layla.2.title: The empty spot
hist.layla.2.hint: The first place in the guide: next to the pyramid.
hist.layla.2.back: Mom was watching an empty patch of sky. “It will come back here.” What will?
hist.layla.3.title: The night I was born
hist.layla.3.hint: A riad where Mom left something for me.
hist.layla.3.back: L-18 is Comet Layla: it comes back every eighteen years, on my birthday. Where is Mom waiting for it?
hist.layla.4.title: The lost phone
hist.layla.4.hint: The darkest sky, next to the red rock.
hist.layla.4.back: Mom lost her phone: that’s why she doesn’t answer. She’s after the darkest sky, in the oldest desert in the world.
hist.layla.5.title: Mom’s telescope
hist.layla.5.back: Mom left me her telescope: “This time, you watch it.” Why isn’t she going to watch it herself?
hist.layla.6.title: The booking
hist.layla.6.hint: The last town before the oldest desert.
hist.layla.6.back: Mom’s backpack is at the hostel, but she isn’t. The comet comes tomorrow. Where is she?
hist.layla.7.title: L-18
hist.layla.7.hint: My birthday night, in the oldest dunes.
hist.layla.7.back: Comet Layla came back, and Mom came walking across the dunes. This time, I found it.
hist.layla.8.title: The most important sky
hist.layla.8.hint: The last page of the guide.
hist.layla.8.back: The last page isn’t blank anymore: a comet and two tiny people on a dune.
hist.layla.1.l1: Mom is an astronomer. Two months ago she left to “observe something,” and she hasn’t answered her phone in three weeks.
hist.layla.1.l2: She left her guide to desert skies on my desk, with a note: “If I’m not back before your birthday, follow the guide. Take the telescope.”
hist.layla.1.l3: Every page of the guide has the same thing written in red: “L-18.”
hist.layla.1.l4: My birthday is in thirty days.
hist.layla.2.l1: Your mom was here a month ago. Every night she pointed her telescope at the same spot, next to the pyramid.
hist.layla.2.l2: There’s nothing there. I looked: not a single star.
hist.layla.2.l3: On her map, that gap in the sky is circled. And next to it: “It will come back here.”
hist.layla.3.l1: Your mom left this at the riad. She said her daughter would come for it.
hist.layla.3.l2: It’s her notebook from eighteen years ago. The last page has my birthday on it.
hist.layla.3.l3: “Tonight I saw a new comet, and tonight she was born. I gave them both the same name.”
hist.layla.3.l4: L-18: Comet Layla, which comes back every eighteen years. This year. On the night of my birthday.
hist.layla.4.l1: Your mom left here ten days ago. She was frantic: she’d lost her phone in the sand.
hist.layla.4.l2: That’s why she doesn’t answer. Nothing happened to her.
hist.layla.4.l3: She said the comet would only be seen properly from the darkest sky, in the oldest desert in the world.
hist.layla.5.l1: At the camp where Mom slept I found her telescope. The big one. She never goes anywhere without it.
hist.layla.5.l2: Inside the case there’s a note for me.
hist.layla.5.l3: “I’ve seen it once. This time, you watch it. The oldest desert is the Namib.”
hist.layla.5.l4: Why would she leave me her telescope? Isn’t she going to watch it? Five days left.
hist.layla.6.l1: The last town before the desert. At the hostel, Mom has a bed booked for tonight.
hist.layla.6.l2: She didn’t show up. Her backpack is on the bed, but she isn’t.
hist.layla.6.l3: She drove off toward the dunes two days ago. She hasn’t come back yet.
hist.layla.6.l4: The comet appears tomorrow night, two hundred kilometers from here.
hist.layla.7.l1: My birthday night, in the oldest dunes in the world. I set up Mom’s telescope and waited alone.
hist.layla.7.l2: At three, the comet appeared in the exact gap from the Cairo map: a line of light over the desert.
hist.layla.7.l3: Then, on the dune across from me, a flashlight blinked three times. Our signal from when I was little.
hist.layla.7.l4: My car broke down twenty kilometers away. I walked all night. You got here before me… just like it did.
hist.layla.7.l5: Eighteen years ago I looked at the sky and you arrived. This time I wanted you to find it on your own.
hist.layla.8.l1: Back home, at night, in Petra. Mom opened the guide to the last page.
hist.layla.8.l2: I left it blank for eighteen years. You know what goes here now.
hist.layla.8.l3: I drew the comet. And underneath, two tiny people on a dune.
hist.layla.8.l4: Good light always comes if you know how to wait. Sometimes it comes walking.
ficha.anaya.likes: Wheelies in her chair, chai with lots of ginger, fabric fairs.
ficha.anaya.fears: That Dadi’s colors fade before she gets back.
ficha.anaya.dreamHint: Marble that turns pink at dawn.
hist.anaya.title: The Lost Color
hist.anaya.1.title: Dadi’s color
hist.anaya.1.hint: It all starts at home: go back to Jaipur, Anaya’s city.
hist.anaya.1.l1: In Jaipur everything is pink, except Dadi’s eyes, which are turning gray. Every day she sees a little less.
hist.anaya.1.l2: She asked me for just one thing: “Sixty years ago I saw a color I never found again. I want to see it one more time.”
hist.anaya.1.l3: It was the scarf of a traveler who passed through her dye shop. Dadi never learned how that color was made.
hist.anaya.1.l4: In the dye book, the traveler wrote a single line before leaving: “If you go looking for it, start in Marrakech.”
hist.anaya.1.l5: I’ve got a chair with wheels, a ticket and a grandmother running out of colors. I’m going.
hist.anaya.1.back: Dadi wants to see, one more time, the color of a traveler’s scarf from sixty years ago. Does it still exist?
hist.anaya.2.title: The tanneries
hist.anaya.2.hint: “If you go looking for it, start in Marrakech.”
hist.anaya.2.l1: The tanneries smell strong and have pits of every color.
hist.anaya.2.l2: I dyed that scarf. Half poppy red, half something the traveler brought from Istanbul and never told me what it was.
hist.anaya.2.l4: I traded it to a Turkish sailor for a rug. Long ago. In Istanbul.
hist.anaya.2.back: The scarf exists: half Marrakech red, half an Istanbul secret. Where is it now?
hist.anaya.3.title: The bazaar
hist.anaya.3.hint: A Turkish sailor and a rug.
hist.anaya.3.l1: The Grand Bazaar has four thousand shops, and in every one they look at my chair. I look at the colors.
hist.anaya.3.l2: My grandfather said the other half of the color was tile dust from the Blue Mosque, ground fine. A blue that turns green in the light.
hist.anaya.3.l4: We sold it to a glass workshop in Venice. They wanted to copy the color in glass.
hist.anaya.3.back: Marrakech red and the blue of Istanbul’s tiles. The scarf went to Venice. Did they manage to copy it?
hist.anaya.4.title: The furnace
hist.anaya.4.hint: A glass workshop that tried to copy the color.
hist.anaya.4.l1: In Murano, glass comes out of the fire like honey. They let me roll my chair right up to the furnace.
hist.anaya.4.l2: We tried to copy that color for fifty years. We never got it: something was missing.
hist.anaya.4.l4: We never found out. We gave the scarf to a Cuban singer who came on tour. She took it to Havana.
hist.anaya.4.back: Not even Murano’s glassmakers could copy the color: something is missing. What?
hist.anaya.5.title: The singer
hist.anaya.5.hint: A Cuban singer who wore it for luck.
hist.anaya.5.l1: Havana is every color at once, as if someone had tipped over a box of crayons.
hist.anaya.5.l2: Oh, that scarf. I wore it at every concert for thirty years. It brought luck.
hist.anaya.5.l3: I gave it to my granddaughter when she moved to Mexico. She paints.
hist.anaya.5.l4: She says she figured out what the color was missing, but she wouldn’t tell me. She says it’s for whoever comes looking for it.
hist.anaya.5.back: The singer’s granddaughter figured out what the color is missing. She says it’s for whoever comes looking: me.
hist.anaya.6.title: The cochineal
hist.anaya.6.l1: Mexico City smells of corn and fresh paint. The scarf hangs in the painter’s studio.
hist.anaya.6.l2: What it’s missing is cochineal: a little bug from the prickly pears that gives the brightest red in the world. The traveler was from here.
hist.anaya.6.l3: But that’s not all. Look at the edge.
hist.anaya.6.l4: Embroidered, tiny: “For the girl from the pink shop in Jaipur.”
hist.anaya.6.l5: The scarf was always meant for Dadi.
hist.anaya.6.back: The scarf was always meant for Dadi: “For the girl from the pink shop in Jaipur.” I have to get it home in time.
hist.anaya.7.title: The color comes home
hist.anaya.7.l1: I came back to Jaipur with the scarf in my lap. Dadi can barely see now.
hist.anaya.7.l2: I put it in her hands. She touched it, smelled it and held it up to the window.
hist.anaya.7.l3: That’s it. That’s the color. I can see it, Anaya. Just a little, but I can see it.
hist.anaya.7.l4: Sixty years waiting for it to come back. And it came back with you.
hist.anaya.7.l5: Every place has a color nobody has named. This one went around the world to come back to its owner.
hist.anaya.7.back: Dadi saw the color again, just a little, by the window. The scarf came back to its owner.
hist.anaya.8.title: A color with a name
hist.anaya.8.hint: Marble that turns pink at dawn.
hist.anaya.8.l1: Dadi wanted to see the Taj Mahal at dawn, even if blurry. We went together by train.
hist.anaya.8.l2: The marble turns pink and then golden. Tell me anyway, I want to hear it.
hist.anaya.8.l3: I told her color by color. Then I gave her a jar: the color of the scarf, dyed by me.
hist.anaya.8.l4: Then it has a name now. It’s called Anaya.
hist.anaya.8.back: The lost color has a name now. Dadi gave it mine.
ficha.cal.likes: The smell of chalk, coffee from a thermos, the sound the Polaroid makes when it spits out a photo.
hist.cal.title: Eli’s Polaroids
hist.cal.1.title: The list
hist.cal.1.hint: It all starts at home: go back to San Francisco, Cal’s city.
hist.cal.1.l1: A year ago Eli fell on the wall while I was holding his rope. He never walked again. And he never spoke to me again.
hist.cal.1.l2: Today his list of summits came in the mail. The one we were going to do together.
hist.cal.1.l3: Seven summits. Next to each one, a space to stick a Polaroid.
hist.cal.1.l4: At the bottom, in his handwriting: “You climb them. I can’t anymore.”
hist.cal.1.l5: Has he forgiven me, or is he saying goodbye?
hist.cal.1.back: Eli sent me his list: “You climb them. I can’t anymore.” Has he forgiven me, or is he saying goodbye?
hist.cal.2.title: Arthur’s Seat
hist.cal.2.hint: First summit: a hill in the middle of the city.
hist.cal.2.l1: Arthur’s Seat is a tiny summit in the middle of the city. I took the Polaroid and waited for the color to show.
hist.cal.2.l2: Then I saw it: another Polaroid tucked between the rocks at the top.
hist.cal.2.l3: The same view, taken a week ago. On the back, a single letter: “E.”
hist.cal.2.l4: Eli can’t climb this. So who did?
hist.cal.2.back: At the summit there was a week-old Polaroid signed “E.” Eli can’t climb. Who was it?
hist.cal.3.title: Table Mountain
hist.cal.3.hint: A mountain with a flat top.
hist.cal.3.l1: On top of Table Mountain, on the lookout railing, another Polaroid signed with an E. Five days old.
hist.cal.3.l2: Yes, I remember. A man in a wheelchair came up in the cabin with a young woman. He laughed the whole time.
hist.cal.3.back: A man in a wheelchair, laughing, with a young woman. Eli? And who is she?
hist.cal.4.title: The steps
hist.cal.4.hint: Steps you climb with your hands.
hist.cal.4.l1: Huayna Picchu has steps so steep you have to climb them with your hands.
hist.cal.4.l2: The man in the wheelchair waited down here. The young woman went up alone, took the photo and ran it back down to him.
hist.cal.4.l3: Her name was Nadia. She said she was his physical therapist.
hist.cal.4.l4: Eli wouldn’t let me visit him for a year. And now he’s going around the world. Why didn’t he tell me?
hist.cal.4.back: Nadia, his physical therapist, climbs for him. Eli is going around the world and didn’t tell me.
hist.cal.5.title: The wall
hist.cal.5.hint: A granite wall over the sea.
hist.cal.5.l1: There’s a rope on the wall of Sugarloaf Mountain. And hanging from it, climbing with just his arms: Eli.
hist.cal.5.l3: I couldn’t. My hands were shaking like that day. I left without a word.
hist.cal.5.l4: That night I got a message from Nadia: “He’s waiting for you at the Middle of the World. He needs to tell you something about the accident.”
hist.cal.5.back: Eli asked me to belay him and I walked away. Now he wants to tell me something about the accident. What don’t I know?
hist.cal.6.title: The knot
hist.cal.6.l1: One foot in each hemisphere. A good place to tell the truth.
hist.cal.6.l2: The knot that came loose was mine. You did everything right. I let you carry the blame for a year because I was ashamed.
hist.cal.6.l3: A year without sleeping, thinking I’d let go of you.
hist.cal.6.l4: That’s why the list: I wanted you to climb without me, and to get there first, so you’d stop looking down.
hist.cal.6.l5: There’s one left. The roof of Africa. And I’m going up it in my chair.
hist.cal.6.back: Eli tied the knot himself. One summit left, and he’s going up it in his chair. Can it be done?
hist.cal.7.title: The roof of Africa
hist.cal.7.l1: Seven days. An all-terrain chair, four porters, and Nadia and me pushing whenever the trail broke apart.
hist.cal.7.l2: This time I held the rope. And my hands didn’t shake.
hist.cal.7.l3: Uhuru Peak. Five thousand eight hundred and ninety-five meters. Take the photo, I’m freezing.
hist.cal.7.l4: The last Polaroid on the list: two guys crying on the summit.
hist.cal.7.l5: One step. Then another. Now I get what it was for.
hist.cal.7.back: Two guys crying on the roof of Africa. The last Polaroid on the list.
hist.cal.8.title: Summits for two
hist.cal.8.l1: Eli’s door is open. The wall of his room is covered in Polaroids.
hist.cal.8.l2: I started a new list. You’re not climbing this one alone.
hist.cal.8.l3: First line: “Any summit, as long as it’s for two.”
hist.cal.8.l4: I took a Polaroid of the list. It hasn’t got its color yet, but I already know how it’ll turn out.
hist.cal.8.back: A new list: any summit, as long as it’s for two.
store.storyNeed: Earned with the secret postcard of {name}'s story.
hist.win.title: YOU WON A NEW OUTFIT!
hist.win.skinSub: Yours forever. Put it on in Clothes.
welcome.2: I run on my own. You don't move me: you build the path I'll run on. Tap a lane and I'll head straight there.
welcome.title: Welcome aboard!
welcome.1: Hi! I'm Nilo. So glad you're here! We're going around the world together.
welcome.3: There are coins along the way. But careful: they only count if we reach the airport at the end.
welcome.4: We use coins to pay for flights on the map. The farther we go, the pricier the ticket.
welcome.5: Each region has its own passport. With the right color equipped, customs will let you through.
welcome.6: If you see a camera on the track, grab it: it's a selfie for the album in your backpack.
welcome.7: And every traveler has a story. Mine starts in my grandma's attic, with Opa's notebook…
welcome.8: Chests and missions give extra rewards. In the shop you'll find outfits and more travelers.
welcome.9: But first, the big question: where do we start? I'm from Berlin, so I've marked it on the map for you… but it's your call!
